sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is an aggressive form of prostate cancer with poor prognosis and limited treatment options. As NEPC aberrantly expresses delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3), the activity of tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager that directs cytotoxic T cells to DLL3-positive (DLL3+) cells, was evaluated in the DeLLpro-300 study (NCT04702737).

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: This was a phase 1b, open-label study evaluating tarlatamab monotherapy in patients with metastatic de novo or treatment-emergent NEPC defined by histologic, genomic, or IHC criteria. Tarlatamab was administered intravenously every 2 weeks at a dose of 100 mg with a 1-mg step dose. The primary objective was safety, and a secondary objective was objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v.1.1; DLL3 expression was retrospectively assessed by IHC.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Forty patients were enrolled (DLL3+ tumors, n = 18; DLL3− tumors, n = 14; and DLL3 unknown tumors, n = 8). The most common treatment-related adverse events were cytokine release syndrome (82.5%), dysgeusia (42.5%), and decreased appetite (40.0%). Cytokine release syndrome was predominantly of low grade (grade 1/2/3/4+, 62.5%/15%/5%/0%), occurred exclusively in cycle 1, and was transient in duration (median duration, 3 days). The ORR was 10.5% [95% confidence interval (CI), 2.9–24.8]; the median duration of response was 7.3 months in the overall cohort. Patients with DLL3+ tumors (vs. patients with DLL3−/DLL3 unknown tumors) achieved a higher ORR [22.2% (95% CI, 6.4–47.6) vs. 0% (95% CI, 0–15.4)] and radiographic progression-free survival rate at 6 months [27.7% (95% CI, 8.7–50.9) vs. 0%].

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: The DeLLpro-300 study provides preliminary evidence for the safety and antitumor activity of tarlatamab in DLL3+ NEPC.

boxed-text.p: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is an aggressive subtype of metastatic prostate cancer with poor survival outcomes. With limited and ineffective treatment options, there is a need for NEPC-specific targeted therapies. In this phase 1b DeLLpro-300 study, the activity of tarlatamab, a delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3)-targeted bispecific T-cell engager, was evaluated in patients using a broad, pragmatic definition of NEPC. The study determined that tarlatamab was tolerable and did not reveal any new safety signals. The study provided preliminary evidence for tarlatamab activity in DLL3+ NEPC. The study supports further investigation of tarlatamab in DLL3+ NEPC and highlights the need for optimization of patient identification and selection in this high-risk and heterogeneous patient group.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is an aggressive subtype of prostate cancer with limited treatment options and poor prognosis (1). NEPC comprises two clinical groups―de novo and treatment-emergent NEPCs. De novo NEPCs are rare and often present with low PSA levels and metastatic disease at diagnosis (2). Treatment-emergent NEPC occurs when adenocarcinoma cells undergo transdifferentiation during treatment with androgen receptor (AR) pathway inhibition (3). A mainstay, first-line treatment for NEPC tumors is often a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen (2). Platinum-based chemotherapy offers limited clinical efficacy, and most patients relapse with resistant disease and short survival (2). Given the lack of approved or effective therapies in NEPC, there is a significant need for new druggable targets for these aggressive and treatment-refractory subtypes of castration-resistant prostate cancers (CRPC; ref. 4).

Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3), a noncanonical Notch ligand, is a downstream target of Achaete-scute homolog 1, a transcription factor that plays an important role in neuroendocrine differentiation (5). DLL3 is aberrantly expressed on the surface of high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas, including 76.6% of NEPC tumors (4) as well as other neuroendocrine marker–expressing neoplasms (6, 7), while maintaining cytoplasmic localization and minimal membrane presence in normal cells (8). Tarlatamab (IMDELLTRA; Amgen) is a half-life–extended bispecific T-cell engager designed with a single-chain IgG construct with binding specificities for DLL3 and cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3) at its N-terminus (9). This enables tarlatamab to bind to both DLL3 on cancer cells and CD3 on T cells, leading to T cell–mediated lysis of DLL3-positive (DLL3+) cells. Tarlatamab induces T cell–dependent lysis of the NEPC cell line NCI-H660, and in preclinical NEPC patient-derived xenograft models, tarlatamab demonstrated significant in vivo activity dependent on DLL3 expression (9, 10).

In a first-in-human phase 1 study (DeLLphi-300; NCT03319940) and subsequent phase 2 study (DeLLphi-301; NCT05060016), tarlatamab demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and potent antitumor activity against previously treated small cell lung cancer (SCLC; refs. 11, 12). Based on the results of the DeLLphi-301 trial, the US FDA granted accelerated approval to tarlatamab for extensive-stage SCLC with disease progression on or after platinum-based chemotherapy (13). The DeLLphi-301 study, based on data from randomized cohorts of 10 mg versus 100 mg, selected a tarlatamab dose of 10 mg intravenously every 2 weeks with one-step dosing for future studies (12). However, at the time of study initiation, the DeLLphi-301 study had not yet identified the 10 mg dose as the recommended dose, and the 100 mg intravenously every 2 weeks with one-step dosing regimen (the highest tolerated dose in the DeLLphi-300 trial) was selected for DeLLpro-300 (13).
DeLLpro-300 sought to examine tarlatamab in patients with previously treated de novo or treatment-emergent metastatic NEPC (NCT04702737).

sec.title: Trial design and oversight
sec.p: The DeLLpro-300 study was a phase 1b, open-label trial evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and antitumor activity of tarlatamab in patients with previously treated metastatic de novo or treatment-emergent NEPC. The highest safe and tolerable dose from the DeLLphi-300 study at the time of study initiation was used with a one-step dose to mitigate adverse events (11, 12). A 40-patient sample size was selected to provide the ability to observe safety events at an incidence as low as 5%. Tarlatamab 1 mg was administered intravenously on cycle 1 day 1 (C1D1), followed by the target dose of 100 mg administered on C1D8, C1D15, and then every 2 weeks. Tarlatamab treatment was allowed after radiographic progression per the Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 (PCWG3) guidelines (14). Radiographic imaging assessments were performed every 8 weeks. Dexamethasone 8 mg was administered before and 1 L of normal saline after all tarlatamab doses in cycle 1.

The trial was funded by the sponsor (Amgen Inc.) and designed by the representatives of the sponsor in collaboration with the investigators. Trial protocols and amendments were approved by relevant institutional review boards and regulatory authorities. Data were collected by investigators and analyzed by statisticians employed by the sponsor. All authors contributed to data interpretation and critically reviewed the manuscript. The trial was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonization Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. All study participants provided written informed consent for the trial.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Patients (male, ages ≥18 years) with de novo or treatment-emergent NEPC defined by one or more of the following criteria were eligible for this study: (i) morphologic evidence of small cell NEPC (ii) positive staining for chromogranin and/or synaptophysin by IHC in >50% of the tumor sample, and/or (iii) ≥2 genetic alterations in tumor protein p53 (TP53), RB1, and/or PTEN observed by IHC or genomic analysis. Eligible patients had disease progression or recurrence after at least one line of systemic treatment: a platinum-based regimen (de novo NEPC) or an androgen-signaling inhibitor (treatment-emergent NEPC). All enrolled patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 to 2. Patients with stable brain metastases were eligible provided they had completed definitive treatment at least 2 weeks (or at least 7 days for stereotactic radiosurgery) before the first dose of tarlatamab.

sec.title: Primary and secondary endpoints
sec.p: Primary endpoints included treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) and treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), and disease control rate evaluated per RECIST v1.1; radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) per PCWG3 guidelines; overall survival (OS); and pharmacokinetics of tarlatamab (15). Exploratory endpoints included retrospective assessment of DLL3 tumor expression. Assessments of safety, rPFS, and OS were conducted on patients who had received at least one dose of tarlatamab. Assessment of ORR, DOR, and disease control rate was conducted per RECIST v1.1 in evaluable patients. Pharmacokinetic analysis was performed on patients who received at least one dose of tarlatamab and for whom at least one sample for pharmacokinetics had been collected. DLL3 expression in tumor samples was assessed by IHC using the Ventana DLL3 (SP347) assay (Roche Diagnostics, catalog number: 08416931001). Positive DLL3 expression was defined by ≥1% DLL3 tumor positivity by IHC. Patients without an evaluable biopsy sample or those who had tumors with <1% DLL3 expression were considered patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors for all analyses.

sec.title: Safety, disease response, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic assessments
sec.p: All TEAEs, TRAEs, and serious adverse events were assessed locally by the site investigator using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v4.0. Grading for cytokine release syndrome (CRS) was conducted per Lee criteria (2014; ref. 16). Immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) events were identified based on a broad search for 61 preferred terms in the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Disease response assessments were made per RECIST v1.1. Calculated pharmacokinetic parameters included time to maximum drug concentration (Tmax), maximum drug concentration (Cmax), and serum half-life (t1/2) of the drug. T cells and cytokines were evaluated using flow cytometry of peripheral blood samples (cytokine measurement: Meso Scale Discovery, cat. # K15049D, RRID: AB_2801398). CD3+ (anti-CD3 antibody: BD Biosciences, cat. # 345764, RRID: AB_2916364), and CD8+ T cell (anti-CD8 antibody: BD Biosciences, cat. # 564116, RRID: AB_2869551) redistributions were measured by differences from C1D1 before tarlatamab dosing. Activation of CD8+ T cells was measured by increased CD8+ CD69+ T-cell subsets (anti-CD69 antibody: BD Biosciences, cat. # 340560, RRID: AB_400523) from C1D1 before tarlatamab administration. Anti-tarlatamab antibodies were analyzed using an electrochemiluminescence-based bridging immunoassay method (MESO QuickPlex SQ 120, RRID: SCR_020304) and followed a two-tier screening assay approach: detecting binding antibodies to tarlatamab and a confirmatory assay. Multiplexed immunofluorescence analysis was conducted on available formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor samples using the MultiOmyx platform (MultiOmyx TIL Panel, NeoGenomics Laboratories).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were used for reporting baseline characteristics, safety, pharmacokinetics, and treatment efficacy. Continuous variables were summarized using means, medians, SDs, and ranges. Confidence intervals (CI) for exact proportions were estimated using the Clopper–Pearson method (17). Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to estimate the medians and percentiles for time-to-event endpoints, with CIs estimated by the Brookmeyer and Crowley method (18). The Greenwood formula was used in CI estimation for landmark calculations (19). Pharmacodynamic biomarker analysis was performed using linear mixed effects modeling from the lmer R package (RRID: SCR_015658; ref. 20). Estimated marginal means and CIs were derived using the emmeans R package (RRID: SCR_018734; ref. 21). Biomarkers were log-transformed and modeled using an interactive term between visit and DLL3 expression status (positive, negative, and not assessed) and a random intercept for subject.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: Amgen has an established process to review research proposals from qualified external medical and scientific researchers. Qualified researchers may request data from Amgen clinical studies. Requests for all data should be directed to Amgen. Complete details, including the kind of data eligible for request, are available at: http://www.amgen.com/datasharing.

sec.title: Patient demographics and baseline characteristics
sec.p: Between June 2021 and November 2022, 40 enrolled patients received at least one dose of tarlatamab (Supplementary Fig. S1). The median age was 64.5 (range, 43–83) years. Patients had received a median of 3 (range, 1–9) prior lines of therapy, with 78% (n = 31) having received platinum-based chemotherapy and 83% (n = 33) having received prior AR-targeted therapy. The median PSA level at baseline was 0.2 ng/mL (range, 0–5,000). Thirty-five (87.5%) patients had visceral metastases, including 26 (65%) patients with liver metastases. A summary of baseline characteristics and histologic parameters is presented in Table 1. The representativeness of study participants is described in Supplementary Table S1. Tumor histology was assessed by either review of local pathology reports submitted (n = 28) or a study pathologist’s evaluation of fresh tissue specimens when a local report was unavailable (n = 9). Tumor histology was not available for three patients. Based on the composite inclusion criteria definition for NEPC (Supplementary Fig. S2), 17 (46%) patients had pure or mixed small cell NEPC morphology, 15 (41%) had adenocarcinoma morphology with positive chromogranin and/or synaptophysin by IHC in a majority of the tumor sample (>50%), and 5 (14%) had non–small cell morphology with ≥2 genetic alterations in TP53, RB1, and/or PTEN by IHC or genomic analysis but without neuroendocrine marker expression.

sec.p: DLL3 expression was assessed retrospectively on submitted tumor samples. Thirty-two (80%) patients had tumor samples evaluable for DLL3 expression. The remaining eight (20%) patients did not have biopsy tissue available for analysis (n = 2) or had biopsy specimens lacking tumor cells (n = 6; patients with DLL3 unknown tumors). Positive membranous DLL3 expression, defined as ≥1% DLL3 tumor positivity by IHC, was observed in 18 (56%) of 32 patients. The percent tumor DLL3 positivity range was 5%–100%. Positive DLL3 expression was identified in 11 (73%) of 15 tumors with small cell morphology (median H-score, 160) and 7 (50%) of 14 tumors with adenocarcinoma positive for chromogranin and/or synaptophysin (median H-score: 105). None of the tumors with genomic markers (TP53, RB1, and/or PTEN) but without neuroendocrine marker expression were DLL3+ (Table 1). The 14 patients with evaluable samples that had <1% DLL3 tumor positivity by IHC (patients with DLL3− tumors) and the eight patients with DLL3 unknown tumor samples were included in the patients with DLL3−/unknown tumor group for outcomes analyses.

At the final analysis data cutoff (July 22, 2024), the median time on study was 6.9 months (range, 1–37) and median duration of treatment was 1.4 months (range, 0.03–35.9). Ten (25%) patients received at least one tarlatamab dose beyond radiographic progression of their disease with a median time of treatment of 1.2 months (range, 0.4–8.1) beyond disease progression.

sec.title: Safety profile
sec.p: TEAEs and TRAEs were observed in all 40 (100%) patients. The most common TEAEs were CRS (82.5%, n = 33), decreased appetite (50%, n = 20), and constipation (45%, n = 18). Other common TEAEs (occurring in ≥20% of patients) are listed in Supplementary Table S2. The most common TRAEs were CRS (82.5%, n = 33), dysgeusia (42.5%, n = 17), decreased appetite (40.0%, n = 16), pyrexia (37.5%, n = 15), and fatigue (35%, n = 14). Grade ≥3 TRAEs occurred in 45% (n = 18) of patients. The most common grade ≥3 TRAEs were fatigue (7.5%, n = 3), hyponatremia (7.5%, n = 3), CRS (5.0%, n = 2), diarrhea (5.0%, n = 2), and lymphopenia (5.0%, n = 2). TRAEs led to dose interruption/reduction in 22.5% (n = 9) of patients and treatment discontinuation in 7.5% (n = 3; grade 3 paramnesia, grade 2 atrial tachyarrhythmia, and grade 4 immune-mediated encephalopathy). The one patient who developed a grade 4 immune-mediated encephalopathy event was identified as having a dose-limiting toxicity. No fatal TRAEs were reported (Table 2).

sec.p: All CRS events occurred in cycle 1 and were predominantly grade 1 (62.5%, n = 25) or grade 2 (15%, n = 6) in severity. Grade 3 CRS occurred in 5% (n = 2) of patients (Fig. 1; Table 2), necessitating high-flow oxygen therapy. There were no CRS events of grade ≥4 severity. The median time between the most recent tarlatamab dose and onset of CRS was 8.1 hours. The median duration of CRS was 3 days, and all events resolved. Outside of supportive care treatments for CRS (antipyretics and glucocorticoids), additional interventions were seldom used, with only two patients each requiring supplemental oxygen or tocilizumab and one patient requiring both. Vasopressor support was not needed for any patient. CRS events led to dose interruption/reduction in 5% (n = 2) of patients and no treatment discontinuations.

caption.p: Occurrence of CRS and ICANS during tarlatamab treatment in patients with NEPC.

sec.p: The overall incidence of ICANS or associated neurologic events was 12.5% (n = 5), with no grade 3 events and one (2.5%) grade 4 event leading to treatment discontinuation (Table 2). All ICANS events occurred in cycle 1, and the median time from the most recent tarlatamab dose to the onset of the first ICANS event was 5.5 days. The grade 4 ICANS event, which occurred after C1D8, was not concurrent with CRS. However, grade 1 CRS had occurred in this patient after C1D1 and had resolved prior to the onset of ICANS. The grade 4 ICANS event was treated with methylprednisolone and tocilizumab, resolved after 5 days, and led to the discontinuation of tarlatamab.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Thirty-eight (95%) patients had measurable disease as per RECIST v1.1 and were evaluable for objective response and DOR. Two (5%) patients did not have measurable disease per RECIST v1.1 but were evaluable for rPFS per PCWG3 criteria. The ORR per RECIST v1.1 was 10.5% (95% CI, 2.9–24.8) and included four patients with partial response (PR). Three patients with PR had treatment-emergent NEPC and had received prior AR-targeted therapy. One patient with PR had de novo NEPC and had received only platinum-based chemotherapy before study enrollment. All patients with objective response had received at least one prior line of platinum chemotherapy. Objective response was observed in three patients at the first planned evaluation (approximately 8 weeks after tarlatamab initiation) and one patient at the second evaluation (approximately 16 weeks). The median DOR was 7.3 months (95% CI, 3.7 to not estimable).

Considering only patients with DLL3+ tumors, the ORR was 22.2% (4/18; 95% CI, 6.4–47.6), and all patients with an objective response harbored tumors that were DLL3+ (% tumor positivity range, 70%–100%; Fig. 2A), including one patient with a durable PR for 35.1 months (Fig. 2A). An analysis of tumor response by DLL3 expression (H-score) revealed a general trend associating greater tumor reduction with DLL3 expression (Fig. 2B). Comparative efficacy results for patients with DLL3+ tumors versus patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors are summarized in Table 3. The median rPFS was 3.5 months (95% CI, 1.9–7.4) for patients with DLL3+ tumors versus 1.7 months (95% CI, 1.6–2.6) for patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors, whereas the median OS was 9.8 months (95% CI, 4.9–15.2) vs. 5.5 months (95% CI, 3.0–13.2; Fig. 2C and D). The Kaplan–Meier estimate of rPFS at 6 months was 27.7% (95% CI, 8.7–50.9) for patients with DLL3+ tumors. None of the 22 patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors had progression-free disease at 6 months. The median time on study and median duration of treatment were longer in patients with DLL3+ tumors versus patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors at 9.6 months (range, 1–37) versus 5.1 months (range, 1–29) and 3.6 months (range, 0.3–35.9) versus 1.4 months (range, 0.03–6.1), respectively. The subset of patients with both DLL3+ tumors and morphologic evidence of small cell NEPC (n = 11) accounted for three of the four objective responses and had a median rPFS of 5.4 months (95% CI, 1.7–7.4) and median OS of 13.3 months (95% CI, 3.2–22.0; Fig. 2E and F).

sec.p: In patients with tumors evaluable for DLL3 expression, CD3+ T cells and CD3+CD8+ cytotoxic T cells assessed in the tumor microenvironment (TME), and with at least one follow-up scan (n = 20), objective response was associated with DLL3 positivity. Whereas there was no significant correlation between increased T-cell infiltrates in the baseline TME and objective response, there was a trend toward improved disease control (Supplementary Fig. S3A and S3B).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: Following intravenous infusion, serum tarlatamab concentrations declined with time in a biphasic manner with a mean (% coefficient of variation) half-life of 6.8 (36) days. Tarlatamab achieved steady-state levels in serum by C2D15. The mean (% coefficient of variation) trough concentrations at steady state (assessed before C3D1 dose) was 4.27 (49) μg/mL. Pharmacokinetics was comparable relative to patients with SCLC (10, 11).

sec.title: Pharmacodynamics
sec.p: Tarlatamab-mediated activation of T cells induced a transient elevation of inflammatory cytokines (including TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10) in T cells after the first tarlatamab dose. Higher induction of cytokines was observed in patients with DLL3+ tumors versus patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors at 2 and 6 hours after tarlatamab infusion on C1D1 (Fig. 3A). Following initial tarlatamab infusion, patients with DLL3+ tumors showed a trend toward greater margination of peripheral T cells versus patients with DLL3−/unknown tumors (Fig. 3B).

sec.title: Immunogenicity
sec.p: During the treatment period, 2 of 39 (5.1%) patients with available postbaseline antidrug antibody data developed treatment-emergent anti-tarlatamab antibodies. Pharmacokinetics of tarlatamab in both patients was comparable with that of patients without anti-tarlatamab antibodies over time. The presence of anti-tarlatamab antibodies did not seem to affect drug exposure levels.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase 1b DeLLpro-300 study of NEPC, tarlatamab 100 mg administered intravenously every 2 weeks with one-step dosing demonstrated no new safety signals and antitumor activity limited to patients with DLL3+ tumors.

Given the bispecific T-cell engager mechanism of action, ICANS and CRS were expected adverse events. ICANS was observed in 12.5% of treated patients, all occurring in cycle 1, with one grade four event leading to treatment discontinuation. CRS was restricted to cycle 1 only and predominantly grade 1 or 2 in severity, with a low incidence of grade 3 CRS (5%). CRS was manageable with standard supportive care measures, including antipyretics and glucocorticoids, with infrequent use of supplemental oxygen or tocilizumab and no vasopressor use. The incidence of CRS (82.5%) in this study was numerically higher than that in the DeLLphi-301 study in patients with SCLC receiving tarlatamab 100 mg (61%), but the incidence of grade ≥3 CRS was similar (6% vs. 5% in this study; ref. 12). DeLLpro-300 used the 2014 Lee criteria for grading CRS, whereas DeLLphi-301 used the 2019 Lee criteria (16, 22). This could have potentially contributed to the finding of higher CRS incidence seen in DeLLpro-300. There is a possibility that the lower 10 mg target dose may achieve an improved safety index compared with the 100 mg target dose studied in DeLLpro-300, although this requires prospective validation.

Patients with metastatic prostate cancer can present with atypical and virulent features of NEPC but without typical histology (possibly because of sampling bias from mixed histology tumors). To encompass this broader group of patients, a pragmatic definition for NEPC was utilized which included tumors with one or more of the following: small cell histology, chromogranin or synaptophysin positivity by IHC, and a definition for aggressive variant prostate cancers characterized by combined tumor-suppressor (≥2 of TP53, RB1, and PTEN) defects (23). Positivity for DLL3 was not an inclusion criterion and was retrospectively evaluated. As previously noted, up to 76.6% of NEPC tumors can express DLL3 (4); however, the definition utilized for enrollment resulted in a cohort that was heterogeneous upon histologic evaluation, wherein only 56% of tumors were DLL3+, likely leading to the limited antitumor activity observed in the overall study population. This is in contrast with up to 94% DLL3 positivity reported in SCLC (11, 24). Intratumor and intrapatient heterogeneity as well as temporal heterogeneity of DLL3 expression (7, 25, 26) in DeLLpro-300 may have led to the numerically lower ORR (22.2% in DLL3+ NEPC) versus that seen in SCLC (40% at 10 mg and 32% at 100 mg in DeLLphi-301; ref. 12). As the majority of NEPC is treatment-emergent, arising from a non-neuroendocrine state, DLL3 expression dynamics in NEPC are likely to differ from those seen in SCLC. In support of this, a study of immunoPET-CT imaging utilizing a novel DLL3-targeted tracer revealed substantial intrapatient and intertumoral heterogeneity in transformed NEPC (26). Taken together with the broad inclusion criteria of this study, these factors may have led to the enrollment of patients with tumors having widely heterogeneous DLL3 expression and consequently an increase in transient or mixed response. Notably, in SCLC, objective responses have been seen in patients with DLL3+, DLL3−, and DLL3 unknown tumors (12). This is different from that seen in NEPC, in which responses were only observed with DLL3+ tumors. Whereas DLL3 expression is a hallmark of SCLC, other neuroendocrine tumors are a heterogeneous group, and the NEPC experience suggests that optimized patient selection strategies might be required for neuroendocrine tumors other than SCLC.

The pharmacodynamic analysis of T-cell margination and activation, production of inflammatory cytokines, and multiplexed immunofluorescence analyses confirmed the heterogeneity and divergent pharmacodynamic response between patients with DLL3+ and DLL3−/unknown tumors. Analysis of DLL3 expression and preexisting tumor-infiltrating T cells revealed a generally immune-depleted TME (consistent with NEPC) and patient response associated with DLL3 expression. Thus, the observed antitumor activity against DLL3+ tumors in NEPC was more likely due to tarlatamab-mediated induction of an immune response versus an innately immune-rich TME primed for response.

Among patients with DLL3+ tumors, those with a small cell histology showed the highest response and seemed to derive the most significant survival benefit. In a prior study evaluating metastatic prostate biopsies of patients whose disease had progressed on AR signaling inhibitors, 17% of patients had morphologic evidence of small cell NEPC that significantly correlated with an increased risk of death (27). Another study noted a shorter median OS in patients with de novo or pure small cell NEPCs compared with those with treatment-emergent or mixed adenocarcinoma NEPCs (28). Whereas only 11 patients in our study had tumors that were DLL3+ with small cell histology, this subset—with potentially the most aggressive disease and least favorable prognosis for survival—achieved the highest survival benefit with tarlatamab treatment and had the longest median survival of all the other patients and remaining subset of patients with DLL3+ tumors.

Limitations of the study included the small sample size and broad NEPC definition that led to a cohort with a wide range of pathologies and DLL3 expression levels that affected the interpretation of response data. The pragmatic approach of utilizing a broad NEPC definition and not including prospective DLL3 selection as an inclusion criterion led to a high number of enrolled patients with DLL3−/DLL3 unknown tumors, limiting the overall study efficacy. This further highlights the need for optimized patient identification in NEPC and the importance of obtaining biopsies in the setting of metastatic CRPC (mCRPC). To enroll a more homogenous population, future studies could utilize prospective central pathology review to confirm histologic features and target expression. Additionally, both fresh and archival biopsies were accepted, resulting in DLL3 expression profiles from some biopsies that were not time-matched to the start of the trial. However, a consistent trend was observed with patients with DLL3+ tumors showing encouraging antitumor activity and survival outcomes that were further enhanced in patients DLL3+ tumors with small cell histology. Other limitations included a possible sampling bias arising from intratumor and intrapatient heterogeneity with respect to NEPC differentiation and the lack of a centralized pathology review that may have led to inconsistent histologic classification. The tarlatamab 100 mg dose was selected as this was the highest safe and tolerable dose evaluated in DeLLphi-300. The selection of the 10 mg target dose in the DeLLphi-301 trial that was ultimately approved for use in extensive-stage SCLC occurred following completion of enrollment in the current study, and this may have led to suboptimal dosing in patients. A 10 mg target dose level may lead to an improvement in the overall balance of safety and efficacy for patients with NEPC as was observed with SCLC (12). An investigator-initiated phase 2 study of tarlatamab in mCRPC, including the use of a 10 mg target dose and more stringent patient selection criteria including requirement for positive DLL3 expression, is planned.

Other DLL3-targeting bi/trispecific antibody therapies that are currently being tested in clinical trials for the treatment of patients with neuroendocrine cancers, including NEPC, are BI-76453, PT217, MK6070 (formerly HPN328), QLS31904, RG6524, and ZG006 (29, 30). Final efficacy and safety results from these trials are awaited. Noninvasive, DLL3-targeting PET-imaging technologies, such as [89Zr]Zr-DFO-SC16.56, can help preidentify patients most likely to benefit from DLL3-targeting therapies and identify intertumoral heterogeneity, allowing for a more accurate assessment of lesion-specific responses (9, 26).

In conclusion, our findings provide preliminary support for the activity of tarlatamab in DLL3+ NEPC and highlight the need for improved approaches to define mCRPC subsets (including NEPC) and identify therapeutic targets in this high-risk population.
